title: Strongly anisotropic non-Kramers electron spin as a quantum coherence probe of angular fluctuations
authors: Achuthan Manoj Kumar, Remy Dassonneville, Guillaume Gerbaud, Nolwenn Le Breton, Athanassios K. Boudalis, Patrice Bertet, Philippe Goldner, Sylvain Bertaina
abstract: Strongly anisotropic non-Kramers rare-earth ions combine giant longitudinal g-factors with a vanishing transverse component imposed by time-reversal symmetry, a combination that makes their spin transitions exquisitely sensitive to the orientation of the applied magnetic field. We show that this sensitivity carries a dual identity: it is simultaneously an overlooked decoherence channel and the basis for a spin-coherence-based angular probe. Using pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance at X-band, we report the first measurements of the quantum coherence of Tb$^{3+}$ in a native-doped CaWO$_4$ crystal (15 ppb) and map the Hahn-echo coherence time $T_2$ as a function of temperature (2 to 10 K) and resonant field ($10^3$ to $10^4$ G). A parameter-free model combining spin-lattice relaxation, instantaneous diffusion and spectral diffusion from all independently quantified impurities overestimates $T_2$ by an order of magnitude at low temperature and wrongly predicts the field dependence of $T_2$, inconsistent with the observed monotonic decrease of $T_2$ with $B_r$. A two-parameter extension, including dynamical angular fluctuations of the crystal axis, reproduces the full dataset across multiple setups and laboratories. Two controlled experiments nominally identical except for different mechanical configuration of the setup establish the mechanical origin of the dominant contribution. The two-parameter extension corresponds to an angular amplitude noise spectral density of overall order 36 n°/$\sqrt{Hz}$ from global external vibrations (ranging from 10 to 66 n°/$\sqrt{Hz}$ depending on the exact setup mechanical configuration) estimated at $\sim$ 2.5 kHz plus a temperature-dependent contribution assumed to come from local phonon-driven angular jitter. It identifies and highlights a decoherence pathway of practical relevance to any anisotropic solid-state spin system.
summary: The researchers used electron paramagnetic resonance on $	ext{Tb}^{3+}$ ions to study quantum coherence, finding that conventional models failed to explain the measured coherence time ($T_2$). They successfully incorporated dynamical angular fluctuations of the crystal axis into their model, demonstrating that ambient vibrations are a dominant, quantifiable decoherence mechanism for anisotropic solid-state spins.
main_problem: To utilize the spin transitions of strongly anisotropic rare-earth ions as a highly sensitive quantum coherence probe for measuring ambient angular fluctuations.
main_result: The dominant decoherence pathway is found to be due to dynamical angular fluctuations of the crystal axis, which can be quantified and modeled by extending standard spin-bath theories.
method: Pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements are used to map the Hahn-echo coherence time ($T_2$) as a function of temperature and magnetic field, comparing results against detailed theoretical models.
model_or_system: The system involves $	ext{Tb}^{3+}$ ions in a $	ext{CaWO}_4$ crystal, which possesses strong magnetic anisotropy ($g_{\perp}=0$). The analysis models the spin Hamiltonian and incorporates contributions from spin-lattice relaxation, impurity diffusion, and crucially, angular jitter.
key_observables: Hahn-echo coherence time ($T_2$), $	ext{EPR}$ linewidth ($\Gamma_{	ext{EFS}}$), and the temperature/field dependence of $T_2$.
important_parameters: Temperature range (2 to 10 K), resonant field ($10^3$ to $10^4$ G), and the angular noise spectral density ($\sim 36 	ext{ n}\circ/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$).
main_assumptions: The initial model failed because it neglected the dynamical angular fluctuations of the crystal axis, which was confirmed by controlled mechanical experiments.
figures_summary: Figures show $	ext{EPR}$ spectra illustrating field-dependent transitions, linewidth measurements ($\Gamma_{	ext{EFS}}$) showing angular divergence, and $T_2$ measurements demonstrating deviations from simple spin-bath models.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical sensitivity of the spin system to orientation, presents initial modeling failures, and culminates in a successful two-parameter extension that incorporates dynamical angular fluctuations to reproduce all experimental data.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, measurable link between solid-state quantum coherence properties and macroscopic environmental noise (vibrations), offering a novel, highly sensitive quantum sensor platform.
